chunks: My father, may Allah be pleased with him, narrated to us, saying: Sa'd ibn Abdullah narrated to us, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, who said:

We were sitting with Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), when a man from the companions said to him: May I be sacrificed for you, O son of Allah's Messenger, do you fear for me that I am a hypocrite? He said to him: When you are alone in your house by day or by night, do you not pray? He said: Yes. He said: Then to whom do you pray? He said: To Allah, Exalted and Glorious is He. He said: Then how can you be a hypocrite while you pray to Allah, Exalted and Glorious is He, not to others?

key_terms.جَعَلْتُ فَدَاكَ: May I be sacrificed for you (a common honorific phrase of devotion)
key_terms.لِلَّهِ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ: To Allah, Exalted and Glorious (indicating exclusive devotion)
key_terms.مُنَافِقًا: Hypocrite (one who outwardly shows faith but inwardly conceals disbelief)

ai.seo_question: How does private prayer indicate sincerity and protect against hypocrisy in Shia theology?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Mani al-Akhbar*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes private prayer (salat al-khassa) as a primary indicator of sincerity, countering the companion's anxiety about hidden hypocrisy. By confirming that the companion’s devotion is directed exclusively to Allah, the Imam highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on the internal state of the heart (ikhlas) over mere outward ritual, distinguishing true monotheism from the dual-mindedness of the munafiqun.
